title: Content with enough
hook: no disaster greater than not knowing what is enough (Tao Te Ching 46)

segments.voice: Yesterday, seems clumsy: chapter forty-five says the greatest skill seems clumsy and the greatest eloquence seems to stammer. Your line was seems clumsy. What did you let look a little rough? Day one thousand one hundred eight.

Two kinds of horses. In the first picture, the fast horses have been sent home to the farms, where they pull carts of manure out to fertilize the fields. Slow, dirty, useful work. In the second picture, war horses are being bred out on the borders, foals born in army camps, far from any field. Chapter forty-six of the Tao Te Ching opens with these two scenes side by side, and says the difference between them comes down to one small thing.
screen: `FAST HORSES PULLING MANURE CARTS.` → `WAR HORSES BRED ON THE BORDER.` → `ONE SMALL DIFFERENCE.`

segments.voice: First, the horses. The chapter says that when the way is followed in the world, the swift horses go back to hauling dung for the fields. When the way is lost, war horses are bred on the frontier. Peace looks humble: a racehorse pulling a farm cart. Trouble looks grand: armies at the edge of the map. Second, the cause. The chapter names it plainly. There's no greater crime than giving in to desire, no greater disaster than not knowing what's enough, no greater fault than wanting to get more. The war on the border starts long before the border. It starts with a want that has no ceiling. Third, the turn. In James Legge's translation, the chapter ends: "Therefore the sufficiency of contentment is an enduring and unchanging sufficiency." Say it slowly. The enough that comes from contentment is an enough that lasts. Other kinds of enough keep moving. Get the raise, and enough moves up with it. Fourth, the other side of a coin. Earlier, chapter thirty-three said that whoever knows they have enough is rich. Chapter forty-six looks at the other side: what happens when nobody knows. Bigger kitchens, fuller closets, longer lists, and the quiet war of always wanting the next thing. The chapter doesn't ask anyone to live with nothing. It asks for one word said and meant: enough. A full plate. A finished day. A home that holds the people in it.
screen: `TWO KINDS OF HORSES.` · `NOT KNOWING WHAT'S ENOUGH.` · `THE ENOUGH THAT LASTS.` · `ONE WORD, SAID AND MEANT.` · then, large: `CONTENT WITH ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one enough. Settle and breathe. Let your eyes or your mind rest on one thing in your life that is, right now, enough. The coat that keeps you warm. The breakfast you ate. A friend who calls. The breath in your lungs at this moment. Name it quietly: this is enough. If you pray, you might give thanks for it. If you don't, just stay with it, and notice if the mind reaches for more. The bell holds the time.
Content with enough. Chapter forty-six: no disaster is greater than not knowing what's enough, and the enough of contentment lasts. Today's word.

Your line: enough is enough. The next time you reach for more today, a second helping, another item in the cart, one more task, pause and ask if you already have enough. Day one thousand one hundred eight.

screen: `DAY 1108 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WITHOUT GOING OUT THE DOOR.`

howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter forty-six as a reminder to name what is already enough, and some keep a habit of pausing before buying or adding more.

fork.reveal: the chapter says no disaster is greater than not knowing what's enough, and the sufficiency of contentment is the one that endures.

original.note: Chinese: knowing what is enough, contentment; chapter forty-six says the enough of 知足 lasts.

trapdoor: what you thought: content with enough means settling for less.
what it means: the enough contentment gives lasts; other kinds of enough keep moving.
what a scholar hears: 知足之足常足矣, the enough of knowing enough is always enough, which Legge renders as 'an enduring and unchanging sufficiency'.
